title: U.S. army to detonate unstable, lead-rich explosives, worrying people in Iowa
summary: The U.S. army will detonate 68 barrels of a toxic lead explosive in Iowa this week on emergency legal powers that allow it to bypass a court order blocking the controversial ‌plan, the Trump…

image.caption: A welcome sign greets visitors to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, where the U.S. army plans to detonate 68 barrels of toxic lead azide later this week. (Zach Boyden-Holmes/USA Today Network/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

The U.S. army will detonate 68 barrels of a toxic lead explosive in Iowa this week on emergency legal powers that allow it to bypass a court order blocking the controversial ‌plan, the Trump administration told a court this weekend.
Army bypassing court order, argues controlled explosion the best choice for lead azide

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit temporarily halted the detonation by freezing the army's environmental permit last Thursday after environmental groups sued to halt the operation. The government said in Saturday night's filing that the army plans to move forward without a permit by invoking an emergency munitions and explosives exception to federal environmental protection laws.
Federal officials say the detonation must ​go forward within the next several days because a drop in temperature could destabilize the material ​and cause an uncontrolled explosion.

"The army must perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion," the U.S. Justice Department said in a court filing late on Saturday.
The army had previously postponed plans to detonate the degraded ​lead azide — an explosive used in military munitions, after public outcry by residents and farmers near Middletown, Iowa.

The Justice Department initially said ⁠the army would act by Tuesday. The U.S. army later said in a post on X that the detonation ‌would take place on Wednesday, "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced."
Lead exposure is dangerous, especially for children
The U.S. army did not respond to a Reuters inquiry on Sunday about the precise timing of the detonation. "Additional details on this situation will be forthcoming," it said in its X post.
Lead exposure can cause serious health problems, particularly in children, including damage to the brain and nervous system.

The Iowa Environmental Council and ⁠the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter filed the lawsuit challenging the detonation, arguing that the detonations would release a toxic plume of lead dust into the air that could travel 160 kilometres north of the site, depending on weather conditions.
Middletown, Iowa, sits on the edge of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

Kerri Johannsen, senior director of policy and programs at the Iowa Environmental Council, told Reuters the army should provide more ‌details about the timing of the detonation, where the plume is expected to travel, and what precautions people should take.

"One of the pieces that especially raised our concerns was the lack of prior notice and the fact that many folks, including state officials, did not have any heads up about this.… There was not enough information being shared," Johannsen said.

The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship has recommended that cattle farmers near the ​detonation site move their livestock, feed and equipment indoors, or transport them to alternate locations. But farmers have told the environmental council that keeping livestock indoors is not a viable option, Johannsen said.
Controlled detonation the lowest risk, army says

In a statement on Thursday, acting ⁠Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the army had determined with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency that a controlled detonation to dispose of the degraded lead was ⁠the option that posed the lowest risk to the public.

Still, the army advised people to avoid the affected area during the detonation and urged anyone ⁠who could ⁠not leave beforehand to stay indoors, close windows and doors, ​and shut off heating and cooling systems that bring in outside air. Residents should wet-clean surfaces children may touch to remove any lead dust once the exposure period has ​ended, the army said.
"The early recommendations from the army had a lot of people sort of with their jaws hanging open.… There remain so many questions about mitigation and protection," Johannsen said.
Jeremy Atwater, a resident of Augusta, Iowa, who plans to leave the area, is shown at the Augusta Community Center on Sunday. (Jim Urquhart/Reuters)
Jeremy Atwater, a resident of Augusta, Iowa, said he planned to head west because he expected the plume would blow south through his town.
"Anything but the bomb," Atwater told Reuters. "It's just going to be a big problem."
With files from The Associated Press
